Best Party Games for Game Night: 5 That Actually Get Played

2026-09-07

I bought Monopoly for my first adult game night. It was a disaster. Three hours of arguing, one broken friendship, and the game still was not done. I swore off board games for two years after that.

Turns out, I was playing the wrong games. Party games are supposed to take 20 minutes, not three hours. They are supposed to make people laugh, not fight over Park Place.

I have run about 40 game nights since then. Some games hit the table once and never again. These 5 are the ones I actually bring out. The ones that survive the night.

1. Codenames. The Word Game That Works With Any Group.

Codenames is the game that convinced me party games could be smart. Two teams. Two spymasters. A grid of 25 words. The spymaster gives a one-word clue to guide their team to the right words. One wrong pick and you lose.

The magic is in the clue giving. You have to find a word that connects multiple targets without hitting the assassin word or the other team's words. It sounds simple until you are staring at a board with "dog, cat, vet, bone" and you need one word that covers three. The tension is real. People lean forward. They whisper. They groan when the clue clicks too late.

I brought Codenames to a family reunion with 12 people aged 12 to 70. Everyone played. Everyone got it. The grandmother was the best spymaster. She won 4 rounds straight. That is when you know a party game is special. $24.97 on Amazon and plays 4-8 players in about 15 minutes. The box is small enough to bring anywhere.

2. Wavelength. The Game That Starts Arguments.

Wavelength is the only party game where you argue about subjective scales. A dial sits on a spectrum between two extremes. "Hot to Cold." "Easy to Hard." "Legal to Illegal." One player sees a hidden target on the dial and gives a clue. The team guesses where the target is.

The first time I played, someone gave the clue "pineapple" for the spectrum "Good Pizza Topping to Bad Pizza Topping." We argued for 10 minutes. The target was right in the middle. Nobody agreed on pizza toppings. That is the game.

Wavelength does something most party games cannot: it makes everyone talk. Not just the loud people. Everyone has an opinion on whether a sandwich is a meal or a snack. The dial mechanic is brilliant because there is no right answer. You are guessing what your teammate thinks, not the truth. It plays 4-8 players, takes 30 minutes, and costs $34.99. Best with 6 people.

3. Herd Mentality. The One Where Copying Is the Goal.

Herd Mentality flips the party game formula on its head. Normally you want to be creative. Here you want to be boring. Everyone writes down an answer to a prompt. If your answer is unique, you get nothing. If your answer matches most people, you score. The pink cow token goes to the most unique answer each round and loses the owner points.

I have seen grown adults panic over the prompt "Name a fruit." They freeze. They cannot decide between apple and banana because what if everyone else picks banana? The pink cow mechanic is hilarious. My friend got the pink cow 4 rounds in a row for answers like "the color blue" when everyone else said red. He was furious. We were crying.

This is the game I bring when I do not know the group well. It breaks the ice faster than anything else on this list. Plays 4-20 players. Yes, 20. It costs $18.23 and plays in 20 minutes. The only downside: if your group has too many contrarians, nobody scores and the game falls flat.

4. Blank Slate. The Word Association Speed Run.

Blank Slate is simple. A card has a phrase with a blank. "Going ________." Everyone writes a word to fill it. If two people write the same word, they score together. That is the whole game.

The surprise is how much psychology is involved. You are not trying to be clever. You are trying to guess what other people would write. "Going fishing" is a safe bet. "Going insane" might score with one person but nobody else. The scoring is team-based so people celebrate together when they match.

I keep Blank Slate in my car. It costs $22.69, plays 3-8 players, and the box is tiny. I have played it at bars, parks, and waiting rooms. It is the most portable party game on this list. One thing: it can drag with 8 players because the matching rounds take longer. Best with 5-6.

5. Sushi Go!. The Card Game That Ends Before You Want More.

Sushi Go! is a card drafting game where you pass sushi cards around the table and try to build the best meal. Pick a card, pass the rest. Simple enough to teach in 60 seconds.

What makes it a party game killer is the speed. Most card games take 30-45 minutes. Sushi Go! takes 15. You play 3 rounds, each round is 5 minutes of frantic picking. The scoring is instant. The art is adorable. Everyone says "one more game" and then you play 4 more.

It costs $11.99. That is less than a pizza topping. Plays 2-5 players and works as a filler between heavier games. The tin box is perfect for travel. If you want a bigger version with more cards, get Sushi Go Party for $24.99. But the original is all you really need.

Here is the part I did not expect: The most expensive game on this list is Wavelength at $34.99. The cheapest is Sushi Go! at $11.99. But the one my group requests the most? Herd Mentality at $18.23. Price does not predict fun in party games. It never does. I have bought $50 party games that flopped. The best ones are the ones that match your group's sense of humor, not the ones with the best components.

How to Pick the Right One for Your Group

Here is how I choose. If the group is quiet and needs warming up, I start with Blank Slate or Herd Mentality. Both are zero pressure. Everyone writes something and nobody has to perform.

If the group is already loud and competitive, Wavelength is the move. The debates get heated. People remember their wins. Codenames is the safe middle ground. It works with any group size, any mood, any energy level.

Sushi Go! is the closer. When energy dips and people want something light before leaving, it is the perfect 15 minute wrap up. I never plan a game night around it. I always use it at the end. It works every time.

What I Wish I Knew Sooner

I spent way too much money on party games that looked good on YouTube but bombed at the table. Monikers, Telestrations, Cards Against Humanity, all the big names. Some worked. Most were one-and-done for my group.

The lesson: buy the games that force talking, not performing. Games where you say one word, guess a spectrum, or match with someone. The performing games (acting, drawing, improv) work for some groups but flop hard with shy people. The word and guessing games never flop because everyone can do them.

Start with Codenames and Herd Mentality. That combo covers almost every group type. Add Blank Slate if you want something portable. Add Wavelength if your group loves debate. Add Sushi Go! if you need a 15 minute closer. You will have a party game collection that actually gets used.
